title: NCSA Gets Supercomputing Capacity With $334 Million Schmidt Sciences Grant
author: Timothy Prickett Morgan

NCSA Gets Supercomputing Capacity With $334 Million Schmidt Sciences Grant

Timothy Prickett Morgan

Timothy Prickett
Morgan

Co-Editor, Co-Founder, The Next Platform

Published
tue 24 Nov 2026 // 18:07 UTC

The National Center for Supercomputing Applications at the University of Illinois is one of the flagship national labs founded by the National Science Foundation more than four decades ago. The NSF-sponsored national labs at were famously goaded into existence by physicist and supercomputing pioneer Larry Smarr, who chose the NCSA name and who ran it for fourteen years.The name is not an accident, and it is meant to focus attention on the applications, not on the supercomputing gear that runs those applications. It is the applications that take on the mysteries of the universe and also, more concretely, solve practical problems in engineering, medicine, and other scientific fields.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

That said, you need increasingly more powerful iron to advance the state of the art in applications, and to be frank, NCSA has not had a very large supercomputer system for quite a long time. But that has changed thanks to a grant from Schmidt Sciences, which has tapped NCSA to install and operate a hybrid CPU-GPU supercomputer based on Nvidia compute engines and networking. The new machine, nicknamed “Garnet,” will have nearly an order of magnitude more performance than the “Delta” and “DeltaAI” systems running in the National Petascale Computing Facility on the Urbana-Champaign campus of the University of Illinois.That datacenter on the Fighting Illini campus was built explicitly in the early 2010s to house the “Blue Waters” supercomputer, which was famously supposed to be an advanced Power7-based parallel supercomputer design from IBM but which Big Blue canceled because the petaflops-class machine would cost far more to build than was budgeted. By my math back in August 2011, when IBM pulled the plug on the original Blue Waters deal, it would have cost around $300 million to build a Power7 Blue Waters machine that delivered around 1 petaflops of sustained performance, which was the lofty goal of the time.And so Cray swooped in with a hybrid CPU-GPU machine, used the same nickname, and NCSA got a very powerful capability-class system for a much more reasonable price of $188 million for the system, funded by NSF as part of an overall $208 million grant for five years of operation. The state of Illinois ponied up $65 million for the NPCF datacenter, and the university put up around $20 million for storage and networking. Blue Waters ran science workloads from February 2012 to December 2019, and the machine was used for national security work until it was shut down finally in December 2021. At launch, the Cray Blue Waters machine had 237 XE6 racks of Opteron 6276 processors and 32 XK7 racks with Nvidia “Kepler” K20X GPU accelerators, all linked with Cray’s “Gemini” 3D torus interconnect and backed by 1.5 PB of memory and 26.5 PB of Cray Sonexion storage. The Blue Waters system had a total peak FP64 processing capacity of 13.3 petaflops and the hardware cost $208 million, which is $15.64 million per petaflops.

Fast forward to the middle of 2027, when the Garnet machine will be installed, thanks to Schmidt Sciences, which is a research and computing organization created by former Sun Microsystems and Google executive Eric Schmidt.Schmidt has a net worth estimated at between $40 billion and $65 billion, and for somewhere around $240 million in hardware costs NCSA will have access to a pair of CPU-GPU machines with an aggregate peak FP64 across its “Grace” CPUs and “Blackwell” GPU accelerators of around 107 petaflops. That works out to a mere $2.24 million per petaflops, a factor of 7X improvement in price/performance and a factor of 8X improvement in performance over the Blue Waters machine from nearly a decade and a half ago.Assuming that the ratio of peak performance to sustained performance on the High Performance LINPACK benchmark is about the same for Garnet as it is for the “Horizon” supercomputer installed at the Texas Advanced Computing Center, which is a Dell machine based on essentially the same Nvidia compute and networking, then Garnet would be rated at about 84.5 petaflops sustained on HPL and would rank at 35th on the current November 2026 Top500 supercomputer rankings. Given the pricing on GPUs and CPUs and DRAM and networking have all gone nuts thanks to the GenAI boom, where too much demand is chasing too little supply, it would take much more money to get a more powerful machine closer to the top of rankings into NCSA.Many of the machines on the Top500 lists for the past several years are based on Grace CPUs paired with “Hopper” H100 or H200 GPU accelerators, which offered good bang for the buck on FP64 workloads. The B200 is respectable on FP64, however, and considering that David Blackwell is a venerated Illini mathematician that the Nvidia GPU is named after, it is only fitting that NCSA moves ahead of the pack to Blackwell GPUs.

Tim Boerner, principal investigator for the Garnet machine and associate director of computing infrastructure at NCSA, sats that the architecture choice and vendor choice was done such that Garnet can be expanded over time but that neither the NSF nor Schmidt Sciences has committed to do so. That said, the intent of the Schmidt Sciences organization is to supplement government HPC funding, not to replace it. So it is not unreasonable to think that the NSF will allocate funds to add future Nvidia systems to Garnet to expand its capacity and therefore its capabilities.There are two parts to the Garnet system. The biggest part is aimed at running both traditional simulation and modeling and AI training workloads and the smaller part is aimed at running AI inference.The biggest partition of Garnet is comprised of 640 of the Nvidia NVL4 system board design, which is one of the HPC-specific designs that has been deployed by a number of HPC centers around the world – including but not limited to TACC, whose Horizon supercomputer is the largest such machine installed to date. The NVL4 design pairs two Blackwell B200s with a single Grace G100s, and then puts two of these nodes on a single system board. (In some cases, all four GPUs and the pair of CPUs can be cross-coupled with NVLink ports to share memory across the six compute units without needing an NVSwitch in the middle, as systems with eight or more GPUs require in the Nvidia architecture.As an aside: Horizon is not just an NVL4 machine, of course, and my math from a year ago says the NVL4 partitions with a total of 4,032 Blackwell B200 GPUs and 2,016 Grace CPUs had a peak FP64 performance of 168.2 petaflops. A Horizon partition with 4,752 nodes of “Vera” Arm server CPUs from Nvidia – so that is 9,504 CPUs and 836,352 cores – delivers another 131.8 petaflops, for a combined 300 petaflops. TACC has lots of CPU workloads it needs to accommodate and has moved gradually, with its users, into GPU acceleration.

In the Garnet system at NCSA, the NVL4 nodes have one 800 Gb/sec ConnectX-8 network interface card per GPU accelerator, and the 640 nodes are interlinked using 800 Gb/sec Quantum-X InfiniBand switches from Nvidia. The machine has a rail-optimized architecture, and it is not surprising at all that NCSA would stick with InfiniBand over Ethernet given its experience with that high speed interconnect and the relatively small scale (in terms of node count) of the Garnet cluster.The smaller part of the Garnet machine is comprised of two NVL72 rackscale machines equipped with Grace C100 CPUs and Blackwell B300 GPU accelerators, which have had their FP64 performance deprecated in factor of jacking up their lower-precision FP8 and FP4 math to better run inference workloads. The two racks have a total of 72 Grace CPUs and 144 Blackwell B300 CPUs, and they have 800 Gb/sec InfiniBand links hooking them together as well as to the other, larger Garnet partition.R. Srikant, director of the NCSA as well as the chief scientific advisor for the Garnet system, tells The Next Platform that some of the $240 million in hardware acquisition costs is allocated to an all-flash storage system from VAST Data that has 50 PB of raw capacity and that will probably have at least 100 PB of usable capacity with de-duplication, compression, and data reduction turned on. This VAST Data storage will augment the existing 25 PB “Taiga” Lustre file system that NCSA acquired from DataDirect Networks.The remaining $94 million or so in funding from Schmidt Sciences will be used to cover five years of operations and research support.Over the course of its scientific worklife, the Blue Waters machine at NCSA supplied more than 39 billion core-hours of capacity to scientists and engineers solving myriad problems. Like other NSF machines, the HPC center hosting a machine gets around 10 percent of the capacity for its local users, and the NSF allocates the other 90 percent according to its own criteria. With the Garnet system, Srikant says that the precise way to allocate resources has not been determined yet, given that the machine is a mix of different kinds of cores, but generally speaking, the same 90-10 rule will apply such that NCSA gets access to around 10 percent of the aggregate capacity for its own work and Schmidt Sciences allocates the rest through its own process. The big difference with Garnet is that researchers outside of the United States will be able to apply for capacity grants – subject to US export controls, of course.Srikant says that NCSA and Schmidt Sciences did competitive bidding for the Garnet machine, and that it had two vendors that submitted bids. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which built the much smaller Delta and Delta AI machines, won the bid. (I am guessing that Dell was the other bidder.) Delta, from October 2022, is a $10 million machine based on HPE’s Apollo server design with AMD “Milan” Epyc processors and a mix of Nvidia and AMD GPUs, from 2020. And DeltaAI, installed in November 2024, is a $14.9 million machine with nearly $30 million NSF grant to build and operate a machine with 608 Grace-Hopper (H200) pairs.As for applications, which again is what these machines are really all about, Schmidt Sciences has its own agenda, and it is particularly keen in sponsoring research in AI and advanced computing systems design, biosciences, astrophysics, and climate modeling.
